questions.stem:
In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, an electron transitions from the $n = 3$ energy level to the $n = 1$ ground state, emitting a photon of wavelength $\lambda_1$. In another transition from $n = 2$ to the $n = 1$ ground state, the emitted photon has wavelength $\lambda_2$. What is the exact ratio of the emitted wavelengths $\lambda_1 / \lambda_2$?
[FIG-stem-chem-bohr-hydrogen-transitions]
(Rydberg formula: $1/\lambda = R_H (1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2)$)
questions.figure_note: Bohr hydrogen atom stationary orbits showing n=1, n=2, and n=3 energy levels with photon emission transitions.

hints.prompt: H1 (Rydberg Formula): State the wave number formula for hydrogen transitions.
H2 (Transition Reciprocals): Calculate 1/lambda_1 and 1/lambda_2 in terms of R_H.
H3 (Crux Move): Formulate the inverse ratio of wavelengths.
hints.text: Crux Move: lambda_1 / lambda_2 = (1/lambda_2) / (1/lambda_1) = (3/4 R_H) / (8/9 R_H) = (3/4) * (9/8) = 27/32.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: An electron in a hydrogen atom undergoes transitions to ground state n_f = 1 from n_i = 3 (emitting lambda_1) and n_i = 2 (emitting lambda_2). We seek the ratio lambda_1 / lambda_2.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: By Bohr's frequency condition and the Rydberg formula, photon wave number is 1/lambda = R_H * (1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2). Inverting yields lambda = (n_i^2 * n_f^2) / [R_H * (n_i^2 - n_f^2)].

3. Execution & Resolution: For n = 3 -> 1, 1/lambda_1 = R_H * (1 - 1/9) = 8/9 R_H => lambda_1 = 9 / (8 R_H). For n = 2 -> 1, 1/lambda_2 = R_H * (1 - 1/4) = 3/4 R_H => lambda_2 = 4 / (3 R_H). The ratio is lambda_1 / lambda_2 = (9/8) / (4/3) = (9/8) * (3/4) = 27/32. Option B is confirmed.
questions.check: Energy check: Since delta E_1 (3->1) = 12.09 eV > delta E_2 (2->1) = 10.20 eV, the photon from n=3->1 has higher frequency and shorter wavelength, requiring lambda_1 / lambda_2 < 1. 27/32 = 0.84375 < 1, which matches physical expectation. Verified.

questions.stem: Consider the isoelectronic series $\text{N}^{3-}, \text{O}^{2-}, \text{F}^{-}, \text{Na}^{+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{Al}^{3+}$. Each ion has exactly 10 electrons ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$). Arrange these ions in order of strictly increasing ionic radius.
questions.figure_note: Radial electron cloud shrinkage with increasing nuclear charge Z for 10-electron isoelectronic series.

hints.prompt: H1 (Isoelectronic Concept): Note that electron screening is nearly identical across 10 electrons.
hints.text: For the same electron count, ionic radius is inversely related to nuclear charge Z.

questions.answer: Official Key: (C) Al(3+) < Mg(2+) < Na(+) < F(-) < O(2-) < N(3-)
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Six ions with identical 10-electron neon configuration: N(3-) (Z=7), O(2-) (Z=8), F(-) (Z=9), Na(+) (Z=11), Mg(2+) (Z=12), Al(3+) (Z=13).

2. Physical Model & Formulation: In an isoelectronic series, shielding constant S is approximately invariant. The effective nuclear charge Z_eff = Z - S increases linearly with atomic number Z. Higher Z_eff pulls the 10-electron cloud tighter toward the nucleus, shrinking ionic radius: r proportional to 1 / Z_eff.
3. Execution & Resolution: As Z increases from 7 to 13, radius decreases monotonically: r(Al3+) < r(Mg2+) < r(Na+) < r(F-) < r(O2-) < r(N3-). This matches Option C.
questions.check: Nuclear pull check: Al3+ has 13 protons pulling 10 electrons (Z/e = 1.30, smallest radius), whereas N3- has only 7 protons pulling 10 electrons (Z/e = 0.70, largest radius). Verified.

questions.stem:
In Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment, an alpha particle with kinetic energy $K = 5.0\text{ MeV}$ ($8.0 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$) is directed head-on toward a stationary gold nucleus ($Z = 79$). At the distance of closest approach $r_{\text{min}}$, all kinetic energy is converted into electrostatic potential energy. Calculate $r_{\text{min}}$.
(Take $1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0) = 9.0 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, charge of alpha particle $q_1 = 2e$, charge of gold nucleus $q_2 = 79e$)
questions.figure_note: Head-on alpha particle trajectory and Coulomb repulsion stopping point r_min near gold nucleus.

hints.prompt: H1 (Energy Conservation): Equate kinetic energy to Coulomb potential energy.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Head-on alpha particle collision with gold nucleus (Z=79, q2 = 79e, q1 = 2e). Kinetic energy K = 8.0 x 10^-13 J.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: By conservation of energy at closest approach (v = 0): K = [1 / (4 pi eps_0)] * (2e * 79e / r_min) => r_min = [9.0 x 10^9 * 158 * (1.6 x 10^-19)^2] / (8.0 x 10^-13).
questions.check: Nuclear scale check: Nuclear radius of gold R ~ 1.2 x A^(1/3) fm ~ 1.2 x (197)^(1/3) ~ 7.0 fm = 7 x 10^-15 m. r_min = 45.5 fm > R, meaning the alpha particle stops outside the nuclear surface due to pure Coulomb repulsion without touching the nuclear core. Verified.

questions.stem: In a gas discharge tube, the specific charge ($e/m$) of cathode rays is completely independent of the residual gas inside the tube, whereas the specific charge ($q/m$) of anode rays (canal rays) varies significantly with the gas used. What is the fundamental physical explanation for this difference?
options: A: Cathode rays consist of neutral particles, while anode rays are positively charged.
B: Cathode rays travel faster than anode rays, preventing interaction with gas molecules.
C: Anode rays are emitted from the metal anode electrode, which varies between experiments.
D: Cathode rays consist of universal electrons, while anode rays consist of positive ions formed from the residual gas, whose mass varies with the gas.
questions.figure_note: Perforated cathode discharge tube illustrating origin of cathode rays vs ionization origin of canal rays.

hints.prompt: H1 (Origin of Rays): Consider where the particles in each stream originate.
hints.text: Cathode rays are electrons stripped from all matter; canal rays are residual gas cations.

questions.answer: Official Key: (D) Cathode rays consist of universal electrons, while anode rays consist of positive ions formed from the residual gas, whose mass varies with the gas.
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Comparison of particle properties between cathode rays (Thomson) and canal rays (Goldstein) in a gas discharge tube.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Cathode rays are fundamental electrons (e-, mass m_e) identical across all elements. Anode rays are gaseous cations created when high-energy electrons ionize neutral gas molecules (M -> M+ + e-).

3. Execution & Resolution: Because different gases have different atomic masses (e.g., H+ vs He+ vs O2+), the charge-to-mass ratio q/m varies inversely with the molar mass of the gas, reaching its maximum for hydrogen gas (H+ = proton). Option D correctly captures this fundamental origin.
questions.check: Historical consistency check: Goldstein observed that canal rays had different deflections for H2 vs air; Thomson verified universal e/m for cathode rays. Verified.

questions.stem: The ground-state electronic configuration of chromium ($Z = 24$) is $[	ext{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1$ rather than $[	ext{Ar}]\,3d^4 4s^2$, and copper ($Z = 29$) is $[	ext{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1$ rather than $[	ext{Ar}]\,3d^9 4s^2$. Which physical factor primarily accounts for this anomalous stability?
options: A: Enhanced stability due to symmetrical distribution of electron density and maximum exchange energy in half-filled and fully-filled d-subshells.
B: The 4s orbital has higher principal quantum number and therefore lower penetration and higher energy than 3d.
C: Relativistic contraction of 4s orbitals causes repulsion between 4s electrons.
D: Chromium and copper atoms form covalent bonds with adjacent atoms in the vapor phase.
questions.figure_note: Exchange energy diagrams showing electron exchange pairs in 3d5 vs 3d4 subshells.

hints.prompt: H1 (Hund's Rule and Exchange): Count parallel spin exchange pairs.
hints.text: For 3d5, number of possible exchange pairs is 5*4/2 = 10, whereas for 3d4 it is only 4*3/2 = 6.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Enhanced stability due to symmetrical distribution of electron density and maximum exchange energy in half-filled and fully-filled d-subshells.
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Comparison of electronic configurations for Cr (Z=24: 3d5 4s1 vs 3d4 4s2) and Cu (Z=29: 3d10 4s1 vs 3d9 4s2).

2. Physical Model & Formulation: In degenerate subshells, electrons with parallel spins can exchange quantum states. The exchange energy is proportional to the number of exchange pairs n_ex = n*(n-1)/2. For 3d5 with 5 parallel spins, n_ex = 10 pairs (a gain of 4 pairs over 3d4 with 6 pairs). Furthermore, half-filled and fully-filled subshells possess exact spherical symmetry, minimizing inter-electronic shielding and repulsion.

3. Execution & Resolution: The stabilization provided by exchange energy (10 pairs) and spherical symmetry exceeds the energy required to promote one electron from 4s to 3d, making 3d5 4s1 the true thermodynamic ground state. Option A is justified.
questions.check: Exchange pair arithmetic: 3d4 has 4 parallel spins -> 4*3/2 = 6 pairs. 3d5 has 5 parallel spins -> 5*4/2 = 10 pairs. The difference of 4 exchange units easily compensates for the small 4s-3d energy gap (~0.4 eV). Verified.

questions.stem: According to the Bohr-Bury scheme, the maximum number of electrons in shell $n$ is $2n^2$, and the outermost valence shell cannot accommodate more than 8 electrons. For the alkaline earth metal Strontium ($Z = 38$), what is the correct distribution of electrons across shells $K, L, M, N, O$?
questions.figure_note: Bohr-Bury shell filling diagram for Strontium (Z=38) showing K, L, M, N, O principal levels.

hints.prompt: H1 (Subshell Filling): Write the subshell configuration first.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Strontium has atomic number Z = 38. We seek the electron population across shells K (n=1), L (n=2), M (n=3), N (n=4), O (n=5).

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Subshell configuration by Aufbau principle is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2. Regrouping by principal quantum number n: n=1 (K) = 1s2 = 2; n=2 (L) = 2s2 2p6 = 8; n=3 (M) = 3s2 3p6 3d10 = 18; n=4 (N) = 4s2 4p6 = 8; n=5 (O) = 5s2 = 2.

3. Execution & Resolution: The shell distribution is K=2, L=8, M=18, N=8, O=2. Total = 2 + 8 + 18 + 8 + 2 = 38. The outermost shell O has 2 electrons (valency = 2, Group 2 alkaline earth metal), perfectly adhering to the Bohr-Bury octet rule for shell N. Option C is confirmed.
questions.check: Sum check: 2 + 8 + 18 + 8 + 2 = 38. Valency check: Sr forms Sr(2+) ion by losing the 2 outermost O-shell electrons, leaving stable krypton core (2, 8, 18, 8). Verified.

Classify the following nuclear pairs into Isotopes, Isobars, or Isotones:
Pair 1: $^{40}_{18}\text{Ar}$ and $^{40}_{20}\text{Ca}$
Pair 2: $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$ and $^{16}_{8}\text{O}$
Pair 3: $^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}$ and $^{37}_{17}\text{Cl}$
options: A: Pair 1: Isotopes; Pair 2: Isobars; Pair 3: Isotones
B: Pair 1: Isobars; Pair 2: Isotones; Pair 3: Isotopes
C: Pair 1: Isotones; Pair 2: Isobars; Pair 3: Isotopes
D: Pair 1: Isobars; Pair 2: Isotopes; Pair 3: Isotones

questions.stem:
Using the Born-Haber cycle for the formation of crystalline sodium chloride $\text{NaCl}(s)$ from its constituent elements, determine the lattice enthalpy $U_{\text{lattice}}$ of $\text{NaCl}(s)$:
$$\text{Na}(s) + \frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2(g) \xrightarrow{\Delta H^\circ_f} \text{NaCl}(s)$$
Given thermodynamic data:
- Standard enthalpy of formation $\Delta H^\circ_f(\text{NaCl}) = -411\text{ kJ/mol}$
- Enthalpy of sublimation of sodium $\Delta H_{\text{sub}}(\text{Na}) = +108\text{ kJ/mol}$
- First ionization enthalpy of sodium $\text{IE}_1(\text{Na}) = +496\text{ kJ/mol}$
- Half bond dissociation enthalpy of chlorine $\frac{1}{2}\Delta H_{\text{diss}}(\text{Cl}_2) = +122\text{ kJ/mol}$
- Electron gain enthalpy of chlorine $\Delta H_{\text{eg}}(\text{Cl}) = -349\text{ kJ/mol}$
questions.figure_note: Born-Haber enthalpy cycle diagram showing gas ionization steps and lattice enthalpy closure.

hints.prompt: H1 (Hess's Law Cycle): Formulate the energy conservation loop.
hints.text: Delta H_f = Delta H_sub + IE_1 + (1/2) Delta H_diss + Delta H_eg - U_lattice.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Born-Haber thermochemical cycle for NaCl(s). Given Delta H_f = -411 kJ/mol, Delta H_sub = +108 kJ/mol, IE_1 = +496 kJ/mol, (1/2) Delta H_diss = +122 kJ/mol, Delta H_eg = -349 kJ/mol.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: By Hess's Law, the direct formation enthalpy equals the sum of step-wise enthalpies: Delta H_f = Delta H_sub + IE_1 + (1/2) Delta H_diss + Delta H_eg - U_lattice. Rearranging for lattice enthalpy: U_lattice = Delta H_sub + IE_1 + (1/2) Delta H_diss + Delta H_eg - Delta H_f.
3. Execution & Resolution: U_lattice = 108 + 496 + 122 + (-349) - (-411) = (108 + 496 + 122 - 349) + 411 = 377 + 411 = +788 kJ/mol. Option B is confirmed.
questions.check: Lattice energy magnitude check: Typical alkali halide lattice enthalpies range from 700 to 900 kJ/mol (e.g., NaCl standard literature value is ~787-788 kJ/mol). Verified.

questions.stem:
An excited singly-ionized helium ion ($\text{He}^+, Z = 2$) undergoes an electronic de-excitation from principal quantum state $n_2 = 4$ to state $n_1 = 2$, emitting a single photon.
[FIG-stem-chem-bohr-energy-levels]
Calculate the wavelength $\lambda$ of the emitted photon (taking $h c = 1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}$ and ground state energy of hydrogen as $-13.6\text{ eV}$), and identify the corresponding electronic transition in a neutral hydrogen atom ($Z = 1$) that emits radiation of the identical wavelength.
options: A: lambda = 121.6 nm; Hydrogen transition n = 2 -> n = 1
B: lambda = 121.6 nm; Hydrogen transition n = 4 -> n = 2
C: lambda = 243.2 nm; Hydrogen transition n = 3 -> n = 1
D: lambda = 91.2 nm; Hydrogen transition n = 2 -> n = 1
questions.figure_note: Bohr energy level diagram comparing He+ (Z=2) and H (Z=1) transitions.

hints.prompt: H1 (Bohr Energy Levels): Write the energy level formula for single-electron hydrogenic ions.
hints.text: For hydrogenic species: En = -13.6 * (Z^2 / n^2) eV. For He+, Z = 2.

hints.prompt: H2 (Transition Energy and Wavelength): Calculate Delta E and lambda.
hints.text: E2 = -13.6 eV, E4 = -3.4 eV => Delta E = 10.2 eV. Wavelength lambda = hc / Delta E = 1240 / 10.2 nm = 121.6 nm.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Match the Rydberg wavenumber in hydrogen.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) lambda = 121.6 nm; Hydrogen transition n = 2 -> n = 1
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A singly-ionized helium ion He+ (Z = 2) de-excites from n2 = 4 to n1 = 2, emitting a photon. We find emitted wavelength lambda and matching transition in neutral hydrogen H (Z = 1).
2. Physical Model & Formulation: In Bohr's model, En = -13.6 * (Z^2 / n^2) eV. For He+ (Z = 2): E2 = -13.6 eV, E4 = -3.4 eV, yielding Delta E = 10.2 eV. Wavelength is lambda = hc / Delta E.

3. Execution & Resolution: lambda = 1240 / 10.2 = 121.57 nm approx 121.6 nm. Wavenumber 1/lambda = R_H * 4 * (1/4 - 1/16) = (3/4) R_H. For hydrogen (Z=1), 1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2 = 3/4 requires transition n = 2 -> n = 1. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Delta E(H, 2->1) = 13.6 * (1 - 1/4) = 10.2 eV. Exactly matches Delta E(He+, 4->2) = 13.6 * 4 * (1/4 - 1/16) = 10.2 eV. Confirmed.

questions.stem: For an electron occupying a $4d$ subshell orbital ($n = 4, l = 2$), determine the number of radial nodes, the number of angular nodal planes, and the maximum number of electrons in this subshell that can possess the spin magnetic quantum number $m_s = +1/2$.
options: A: Radial nodes = 1, Angular nodes = 2, Max electrons (ms = +1/2) = 5
B: Radial nodes = 2, Angular nodes = 1, Max electrons (ms = +1/2) = 5
C: Radial nodes = 1, Angular nodes = 2, Max electrons (ms = +1/2) = 10
D: Radial nodes = 0, Angular nodes = 2, Max electrons (ms = +1/2) = 5

hints.prompt: H1 (Nodal Formulas): Recall the formulas for radial and angular nodes in hydrogenic wavefunctions.
hints.text: Number of radial (spherical) nodes = n - l - 1. Number of angular nodal planes = l.

hints.prompt: H2 (Degeneracy of d Subshell): Count the number of orbitals in l = 2.
hints.text: For l = 2, magnetic quantum numbers are ml = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2 (5 distinct orbitals).

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Apply Pauli Exclusion Principle to count max electrons with ms = +1/2.
hints.text: Crux Move: Each of the 5 orbitals can hold at most 1 electron with spin ms = +1/2. Maximum such electrons = 5.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Radial nodes = 1, Angular nodes = 2, Max electrons (ms = +1/2) = 5
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A 4d orbital has principal quantum number n = 4 and azimuthal quantum number l = 2. We determine radial nodes, angular nodes, and max electrons with ms = +1/2.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Radial nodes = n - l - 1 = 4 - 2 - 1 = 1. Angular nodes = l = 2. Total nodes = n - 1 = 3. A d subshell has 2l + 1 = 5 degenerate orbitals.

3. Execution & Resolution: By the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule, each of the 5 orbitals can host at most one electron with spin ms = +1/2. Thus, maximum electrons with ms = +1/2 is 5. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Total nodes = 1 + 2 = 3 = n - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3. Total capacity = 10, half with +1/2 = 5. Confirmed.

questions.stem: The first ionization enthalpies ($\text{IE}_1$) of the second-period elements exhibit two notable anomalies against the general increasing trend with nuclear charge: $\text{IE}_1(\text{Be}) > \text{IE}_1(\text{B})$ and $\text{IE}_1(\text{N}) > \text{IE}_1(\text{O})$. Which statement correctly justifies both anomalies based on subshell electronic configurations?
options: A: Be ([He] 2s^2) loses an electron from a fully filled penetrating 2s subshell while B ([He] 2s^2 2p^1) loses an electron from an easily shielded higher-energy 2p subshell; N ([He] 2s^2 2p^3) has extra exchange stability from a half-filled 2p subshell while O ([He] 2s^2 2p^4) experiences inter-electronic repulsion in a paired 2p orbital.
B: Be has a higher nuclear charge than B, and N has a higher nuclear charge than O.
C: B has higher electronegativity than Be, and O has higher electron affinity than N.
D: 2p electrons in Be penetrate closer to the nucleus than 2s electrons in B.

hints.prompt: H1 (Configuration of Be vs B): Compare subshells from which electrons are removed in Be and B.
hints.text: Be: [He] 2s^2 (loss of 2s electron). B: [He] 2s^2 2p^1 (loss of 2p electron). 2s electrons have greater orbital penetration and shield the 2p electron.

hints.prompt: H2 (Configuration of N vs O): Compare 2p subshell electron arrangements in N and O.
hints.text: N: [He] 2s^2 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1 (symmetrically half-filled 2p subshell with high exchange energy). O: [He] 2s^2 2p_x^2 2p_y^1 2p_z^1 (contains a paired orbital).

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Combine subshell penetration and spin pairing repulsions.
hints.text: Crux Move: Full-filled 2s stability in Be exceeds single 2p in B; spin pairing repulsion in O facilitates electron removal compared to half-filled exchange stability in N.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Be ([He] 2s^2) loses an electron from a fully filled penetrating 2s subshell while B ([He] 2s^2 2p^1) loses an electron from an easily shielded higher-energy 2p subshell; N ([He] 2s^2 2p^3) has extra exchange stability from a half-filled 2p subshell while O ([He] 2s^2 2p^4) experiences inter-electronic repulsion in a paired 2p orbital.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: In Be (2s^2), the 2s electron experiences greater penetration and effective nuclear charge than the 2p electron in B (2s^2 2p^1), which is shielded by inner 2s electrons. In N (2p^3), all three 2p orbitals are singly occupied, maximizing quantum exchange energy.

B: CO2 and SO2; Central atom has 0 lone pairs in CO2 and 1 lone pair in SO2

B: H2O has covalent bonds while H2S, H2Se, and H2Te are ionic compounds.

[FIG-stem-chem-amphoteric-oxide-reaction]

questions.stem:
Four metal strips $P, Q, R, S$ are tested with aqueous solutions of their respective sulfates ($P\text{SO}_4, Q\text{SO}_4, R\text{SO}_4, S\text{SO}_4$). It is observed that:
1. Metal $Q$ displaces $P, R,$ and $S$ from their salt solutions.
2. Metal $P$ displaces $R$ and $S$, but cannot displace $Q$.
3. Metal $S$ displaces $R$, but cannot displace $P$ or $Q$.

B: Q > S > P > R; Metal Q

D: Q > P > R > S; Metal S

hints.text: Obs 1: Q > P, Q > R, Q > S. Obs 2: P > R, P > S, but Q > P. Obs 3: S > R.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Synthesize the linear ordering.
hints.text: Crux Move: Combining inequalities gives Q > P > S > R. The most reactive metal (Q) reacts most vigorously with dilute acid.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Q > P > S > R; Metal Q

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Q displaces P, R, S => Q is highest. P displaces R, S => P > R, S. S displaces R => S > R. Combining yields Q > P > S > R.
3. Execution & Resolution: The reactivity sequence is strictly Q > P > S > R. Metal Q has the highest oxidation potential and evolves H2 most vigorously with dilute acid. Option A.

The elements of the second period of the Modern Periodic Table in order of increasing atomic number are: $\text{Li}, \text{Be}, \text{B}, \text{C}, \text{N}, \text{O}, \text{F}, \text{Ne}$. Although ionization energy generally increases across a period from left to right due to increasing nuclear charge, two distinct anomalies occur in this period:
1. $\text{IE}_1(\text{Be}) > \text{IE}_1(\text{B})$
2. $\text{IE}_1(\text{N}) > \text{IE}_1(\text{O})$
Which of the following correctly accounts for these two anomalies based on electronic configuration stability, and presents the strictly correct increasing order of First Ionization Energy ($\text{IE}_1$) across the second period?
options: A: Be has a fully-filled 2s² subshell and N has a half-filled 2p³ subshell of extra stability; Order: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne
B: Be has higher nuclear charge than B and N has higher electronegativity than O; Order: Li < Be < B < C < N < O < F < Ne
C: B loses a core electron while O undergoes shielding; Order: Li < B < Be < C < N < O < F < Ne
D: Be has a fully-filled 2s² subshell but O has pairing stability; Order: Li < Be < B < C < O < N < F < Ne

questions.stem: An alcohol (A) on dehydration with concentrated H2SO4 at a high temperature yields compound (B). On ozonolysis every molecule of compound (B) yields two molecules of acetaldehyde. Which of the following is the starting alcohol (A)?

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Reductive ozonolysis cleaves an alkene double bond into carbonyl fragments. Producing two molecules of acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) identifies the symmetric intermediate alkene as but-2-ene (CH3-CH=CH-CH3).

2. Reaction Pathway Evaluation: Dehydration of 2-butanol with concentrated H2SO4 under high temperature gives but-2-ene via Saytzeff elimination. Dehydration of 1-butanol under strongly acidic thermal conditions also produces but-2-ene via carbocation rearrangement. The official key explicitly accepts both alcohols.
3. Conclusion: The starting alcohol is either 1-butanol or 2-butanol. Hence Option A OR B.

questions.stem: In an experiment with 100 mL 0.1 M solution of Copper Chloride, by mistake 5 g of a mixture containing equal weights of Tin, Silver, Lead and Calcium was added. Finally, after some time, the solution gets completely decolourised. This is mainly due to:
options: A: Silver reacts with copper chloride.
B: Calcium reacts with copper chloride.
C: All the metals react with copper chloride.
D: Only lead reacts with copper chloride, forming white precipitate of lead chloride.

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: The characteristic blue color of aqueous copper chloride is due to hydrated Cu2+ ions. Complete decolourisation requires quantitative single-displacement redox by an electropositive metal higher in the activity series.

2. Stoichiometric Mass Balance: Solution contains 0.100 L * 0.1 M = 0.010 mol CuCl2. The mixture contains 1.25 g calcium (0.031 mol Ca). Since calcium is highly electropositive (Ca -> Ca2+ + 2e-), 0.031 mol Ca is more than sufficient to displace all 0.010 mol Cu2+ (Ca + CuCl2 -> CaCl2 + Cu), removing the blue color. Silver does not displace copper.
3. Conclusion: The decolourisation is primarily due to calcium reacting with copper chloride. Hence Option B.

questions.stem: Triclosan (C12H7Cl3O2) is an antibacterial and antifungal agent. It is a polychloro phenoxy phenol. It is widely used as a preservative and antimicrobial agent in personal care products such as soaps, skin creams, and deodorants etc. A label on a 200 mL hand-sanitizer bottle claims that it contains Triclosan 0.2% w/v. What will be the number of molecules of Triclosan present in the bottle? (NA is Avogadro's Number.)

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: A 0.2% w/v solution contains 0.2 g solute per 100 mL solution. Moles equals mass divided by molar mass, and molecules equals moles multiplied by Avogadro's number.

2. Quantitative Proof of Error: In 200 mL, mass of triclosan (C12H7Cl3O2, M = 289.5 g mol^-1) is 0.4 g. Moles = 0.4 / 289.5 = 1.38 * 10^-3 mol. Number of molecules is 1.38 * 10^-3 NA. All printed options feature severe exponent errors (10^22 NA to 10^25 NA). Consequently, IAPT officially dropped this question.
3. Conclusion: Officially dropped by IAPT. Official status: DROP.

questions.stem: Suppose that A and B form compounds B2A3 and B2A. If 0.05 mole of B2A3 weighs 12 g and 0.1 mole of B2A weighs 10 g, what are the atomic weights of A and B respectively?

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Compound molar mass equals the linear combination of constituent atomic weights multiplied by their stoichiometric subscripts.

2. Quantitative Proof of Error: For B2A3: 0.05 mol weighs 12 g implies molar mass = 240 g mol^-1, so 2B + 3A = 240. For B2A: 0.1 mol weighs 10 g implies molar mass = 100 g mol^-1, so 2B + A = 100. Subtracting yields 2A = 140, so A = 70. Then 2B = 30, so B = 15. The authentic atomic weights are A = 70 and B = 15, which are missing from the options. Consequently, IAPT officially dropped this question.
3. Conclusion: Officially dropped by IAPT. Official status: DROP.

questions.stem: Acetylene torches and burners used by glassblowers produce intense ultraviolet light. Glassblowers wear special glasses that contain which of the following elements to absorb the UV?

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Didymium is a mixture of lanthanoid rare-earth elements, primarily neodymium (Nd) and praseodymium (Pr).

2. Spectroscopic Absorption: Neodymium and praseodymium oxides have sharp optical absorption bands that effectively filter out blinding sodium D-line flare (589 nm) and intense ultraviolet radiation produced by high-temperature glassblowing torches.
3. Conclusion: Glassblowers' safety glasses contain neodymium and praseodymium. Hence Options A, B.

questions.stem: Equal lengths of magnesium ribbons are taken in four test tubes A, B, C and D. In test tube A, 1 M acetic acid is added; in test tube B, 1 M HCl is added; in test tube C, 1 M HNO3 is added; and in test tube D, 1 M NaOH is added. The observed results will be:
options: A: Fizzing occurs more vigorously in A.
B: Fizzing occurs more vigorously in B.
C: Fizzing occurs more vigorously in C.
D: Fizzing occurs more vigorously in D. 9

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: The rate of hydrogen gas evolution in single displacement reactions of magnesium metal is governed by active hydrogen ion concentration [H+] and acid strength.

2. Comparative Acid-Base Dynamics: Test tube A (1 M acetic acid) is a weak organic acid with slight dissociation, resulting in slow fizzing. Test tube B (1 M HCl) is a completely dissociated strong mineral acid, causing rapid vigorous hydrogen fizzing. Test tube C (1 M HNO3) is a strong oxidising acid reacting vigorously with magnesium to liberate gas. Test tube D (1 M NaOH) is an alkaline base that does not react with magnesium under room conditions.
3. Conclusion: Fizzing occurs vigorously in test tubes B and C. Hence Options B, C.
